content:
Time travel is the concept of moving between certain points in time. Time travel mostly involves a hypothetical device known as a time machine. It is a widely known concept in philosophy and fiction, particularly science fiction. H.G. Wells’ 1895 novel The Time Machine set the genre alight. In general, time travel stories focus on the effects of trekking into the past or future. The central premise for these stories often involves changing history, either intentionally or by accident. They focus on how altering the past changes the future and creates an altered present or future for the time traveler upon their return home. In other instances, the premise is that the past cannot be changed or that the future is predetermined. As a result, the protagonist's actions are either inconsequential or intrinsic to events as they originally unfolded. Some stories focus solely on the paradoxes and alternate timelines that come with time travel.

Time travel stories from antiquity often featured time travel into the future by sleeping. In other cases, time travel into the past happened through supernatural means by angels or spirits. Some ancient myths depict a character skipping forward in time. In Hindu mythology, the Vishnu Purana mentions the story of King Raivata Kakudmi, who travels to heaven to meet the creator Brahma. When he returns, he is surprised that millennia have passed. The Japanese tale of "Urashima Tarō" tells of a young fisherman named Urashima-no-ko who visits an undersea palace. After three days, he returns home to his village and finds himself 300 years in the future. He has been forgotten, his house is in ruins, and his family has died. In Jewish tradition, the 1st-century BCE scholar Honi ha-M'agel fell asleep for seventy years. When he woke up and returned home, he found no one he knew. No one believed his claims of time travel.

Time travel in modern fiction can be achieved by space and time warps. This stems from the scientific theory of general relativity. Math is also used in science fiction. Chaos theory states that within the randomness of complex systems, there are patterns, feedback loops, repetition, fractals, and self-organization. The butterfly effect is a basic principle of chaos. It is the notion that small events can have large, widespread impacts. The idea describes events observed where a very small change in initial conditions results in vastly distinct outcomes. Mathematician Edward Lorenz coined the term. A metaphor for this theory is that a butterfly flapping its wings in Brazil can cause a tornado in Texas. This “butterfly effect” appears in modern fiction. For example, in Ray Bradbury's 1952 short story A Sound of Thunder, killing a single insect millions of years in the past greatly changes the world.

Time travel isn’t just something we read about in science fiction. Some theories, most notably special and general relativity, suggest that some geometries of space-time or specific types of motion in space might allow time travel.  Physicists discuss the possibility of closed timelike curves. These curves form closed loops in space-time, allowing objects to return to their own past. There are known solutions to the equations of general relativity that describe space-times that contain closed timelike curves, such as Gödel space-time. Yet, the likelihood of these ideas is uncertain. Most physicists believe that backward time travel is highly unlikely. Any theory that would allow time travel would cause problems of causality. A classic example of this is the "grandfather paradox." This involves traveling to the past and intervening in the birth of one's ancestors. That means causing the death of an ancestor before their birth.
